content: The purpose of this review is to evaluate two key aspects of HIV self-testing (HIVST): (1) the diverse values and preferences of key populations (KP) regarding HIVST as documented in the literature, and (2) the level of acceptability of HIVST among these populations. HIVST is considered a promising strategy to address disparities in access to and uptake of HIV testing, particularly among KP. A literature review was conducted to assess the acceptability, values, and preferences of KP regarding HIVST. The data were analyzed based on factors such as country income classification (as per the World Bank), type of specimen collection, level of support provided, and other qualitative aspects. The majority of studies reviewed originated from high-income countries and primarily involved men who have sex with men (MSM). These studies generally found HIVST to be acceptable among MSM. MSM participants expressed interest in HIVST due to its convenience and privacy. However, concerns were raised about the lack of counseling, potential user errors, and the accuracy of the tests. Limited data are available on the values and preferences of other KP groups regarding HIVST, highlighting the need for further research, especially as HIVST becomes more widely available, including in resource-limited settings. Key populations are disproportionately affected by HIV, with pooled HIV prevalence rates 10 to 50 times higher than those in the general population. Globally, over two million new HIV infections occur annually, with an estimated 40% of new adult HIV infections occurring among KP. Despite the high burden of HIV and the increasing global coverage of HIV testing and treatment services, KP remain underserved. HIVST involves the process of self-collecting a specimen, self-performing the test, and self-interpreting the result to determine one’s HIV status. HIVST has the potential to increase demand for and uptake of HIV testing services (HTS) among KP, who may be reluctant or unable to access existing services, thereby reducing disparities in HIV testing coverage and access. Understanding the values and preferences of KP regarding HIVST is critical to realizing the potential impact of self-testing as part of the global HIV response. Values and preferences are defined as participants’ views on HIVST, their concerns about the process, their willingness to pay for or purchase an HIV self-test, and their opinions on test kits specifically packaged for HIVST or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) used for self-testing. Acceptability of HIVST refers to participants’ willingness to use the test in the future or to increase the frequency of testing using a home-based HIV test. Currently, only one rapid diagnostic test is approved for over-the-counter sale and specifically packaged for self-testing by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA). However, the development of HIVST policies and the availability of testing vary across countries. Reports suggest that HIV RDTs have been informally available for self-testing for some time, and their use is increasing, particularly among KP. The primary method for identifying studies was electronic searches conducted in five international databases (PubMed, PopLine, Scopus, EMBASE, and PsycINFO) and five major HIV/AIDS conference databases for publications between January 1995 and July 2014. Gray literature, defined as reports produced by various entities but not controlled by commercial publishers, was identified through comprehensive Google searches. The electronic searches were supplemented with bibliographic back-referencing. The search terms included combinations of “HIV,” “self-testing,” “home testing,” and “rapid testing.” The search was restricted to human subjects, with no language or geographic limitations. Abstracts were included if full-text articles were unavailable. Studies were included if they used original data, involved at least one of the five KP groups (MSM, sex workers, transgender people, people who inject drugs, and people in prison), and employed qualitative and/or quantitative methods to evaluate any aspect of HIVST values and preferences. Studies that did not meet these criteria were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened studies, and disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. The quality of studies was assessed using appropriate checklists for the study designs. Data were summarized qualitatively based on study design, methodology, location, resources, and population. Extracted data were coded by country income classification, educational level, type of specimen collection (oral fluid-based, blood-based, or unspecified), KP group, and type of support provided (supervised, unsupervised, or unspecified). Acceptability was categorized as high (≥67%), moderate (34–66%), or low (≤33%). Approaches to HIVST were defined according to the 2014 WHO and UNAIDS technical update on HIV self-testing. Supervised approaches involved direct support from a health worker or volunteer before or after self-testing, while unsupervised approaches did not require direct support but could include information on accessing support services. Studies with no information or comparing different approaches or specimen collection methods were analyzed separately. The review identified 2,156 citations, of which 158 were retrieved for further analysis. After excluding irrelevant articles, 23 studies were included in the final review. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, with participants ranging in age from 13 to 76 years. Education levels were reported in 14 studies, with more than half of the participants in 11 studies having at least a college education. Sample sizes ranged from 27 to 5,908 participants. Thirteen studies used oral fluid-based HIV RDTs, five used blood-based RDTs, three used both types, and two did not specify the type of specimen collection. Nine studies used an unsupervised approach, seven used a supervised approach, six did not report this information, and one compared both approaches. Out of 14 studies evaluating acceptability, eight reported high acceptability, five reported moderate acceptability, and one reported low acceptability. Acceptability rates ranged from 21% to 98%. MSM were included in all studies, and three studies included female sex workers (FSW). In Kenya, FSW reported higher acceptability (98%) compared to MSM (57%). No significant differences in acceptability were identified across different approaches, specimen collection methods, country income levels, KP groups, or educational levels. The benefits of HIVST reported in 18 studies included convenience, privacy, ease of use, and being painless. Convenience and privacy were the most frequently reported benefits, followed by ease of use and being painless. Privacy was more commonly reported as a benefit in studies using an unsupervised approach compared to a supervised approach. Participants generally preferred oral fluid-based HIV RDTs over blood-based RDTs. Preferences for HIVST attributes varied across country income settings, approaches, and specimen collection methods. In conclusion, HIVST has the potential to address disparities in HIV testing access and uptake among KP. However, further research is needed to understand the values and preferences of diverse KP groups, particularly in resource-limited settings, to optimize the implementation and impact of HIVST.
